## 📖 Course overview

This course is written for graduate students with a **wet-lab background** and little or no computational experience.

Over seven weeks we walk up the central dogma: genome ➡️ epigenome ➡️ transcriptome ➡️ single-cell resolution ➡️ proteome ➡️ microbiome — asking the same three questions of every technology.

> **① What does the assay actually measure?** **② What does the data look like?** **③ What can go wrong?**

::: {layout-ncol="2"}
### What this course is

✅ Concepts, interpretation, and study design\
✅ How to read a methods section and judge whether to believe a figure\
✅ Enough vocabulary to have a productive conversation with a bioinformatician

### What this course is **not**

❌ A programming course. There is no R or Python here.\
❌ A pipeline tutorial. Tool names appear only as landmarks.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The practical course

A separate **hands-on bioinformatics practicum** is offered next semester. This course is its conceptual prerequisite — the goal here is that you know *what* you want to compute before you learn *how*.
:::

## 🗓️ Syllabus

| Week   | Topic                                                     | Central question                                             |
+:======:+===========================================================+==============================================================+
| **W1** | [Introduction to Bioinformatics](chapters/w1_intro.qmd)   | You just generated 200 GB of sequencing data.\               |
|        |                                                           | What now?                                                    |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+

## 📑 What is inside each week

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W1 · Introduction to Bioinformatics

1.  What Bioinformatics Is 👩‍💻 — the three neighbouring fields; wet lab ➡️ dry lab; the five-stage omics workflow that maps the whole course
2.  Sequencing and Data 🧪 — Sanger, short-read, long-read; FASTQ / BAM / VCF / count matrix; the reference genome and reference bias
3.  Where the Data Lives 🗄️ — GEO, SRA, dbGaP, UK Biobank, GTEx, ENCODE, TCGA, HCA
4.  Statistics You Cannot Avoid 📊 — p-values, multiple testing, batch effects, power
5.  Reproducibility and Study Design ♻️ — the conversation to have *before* you sequence
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W2 · Genomics

1.  Human Genetic Variation 🧬 — SNVs, SVs, repeats; allele frequency and allelic architecture
2.  From Reads to Variants 🔬 — variant calling as inference; WGS vs WES vs array; imputation
3.  Genome-Wide Association Studies 📈 — population structure, the association test, Manhattan and QQ plots, 5×10⁻⁸, linkage disequilibrium
4.  From Association to Function 🔎 — fine-mapping, credible sets, eQTL, colocalization, TWAS
5.  Heritability and Prediction 🧮 — SNP heritability, polygenicity, polygenic risk scores
6.  Genomics in the Clinic 🏥 — cancer genomics, Mendelian randomization, drug target discovery
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W3 · Epigenomics

1.  What the Epigenome Is 🎛️ — four layers, four assays; one epigenome per cell type
2.  DNA Methylation 🔵 — bisulfite vs arrays, β and M values, DMPs and DMRs, epigenetic clocks
3.  Histone Modifications and ChIP-seq 🧵 — what the marks mean, input controls, peak calling
4.  Chromatin Accessibility: ATAC-seq 🔓 — the assay, its QC, and footprinting
5.  Reading the Regulatory Genome 📖 — motifs, ChromHMM, ENCODE/Roadmap, Hi-C and TADs
6.  Why This Matters Clinically 🏥 — the bridge from non-coding GWAS hits to mechanism
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W4 · Transcriptomics

1.  What RNA-seq Measures 📏 — abundance, not synthesis; and not protein
2.  Experimental Choices ⚙️ — poly(A) vs rRNA depletion, strandedness, replicates, design checklist
3.  From Reads to Counts 🔢 — spliced alignment vs pseudo-alignment; gene vs transcript level
4.  Normalization ⚖️ — library size, gene length, and the composition effect; CPM/TPM/TMM/RLE
5.  Differential Expression 📊 — the negative binomial model, shrinkage, sample size, volcano and MA plots
6.  Making Sense of a Gene List 🧠 — ORA vs GSEA and the three commonest misuses
7.  Beyond Differential Expression 🌐 — WGCNA, deconvolution, splicing, eQTLs
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W5 · Single-cell Transcriptomics

1.  Why Single Cell 🔬 — what averaging destroys, and when bulk is still better
2.  Platforms and Sample Choices 🧫 — droplet vs plate vs combinatorial; cells vs nuclei
3.  From Droplets to a Count Matrix 🧮 — barcodes, UMIs, zeros, and QC
4.  Finding Cell Types 🗺️ — HVGs, PCA, UMAP, clustering resolution, annotation
5.  Batch Effects and Integration 🔗 — Harmony/scVI, and over-correction
6.  Statistical Testing 📊 — why per-cell tests are invalid; pseudobulk; differential abundance
7.  Dynamics, Space, and Atlases 🌈 — trajectories, cell–cell communication, spatial, HCA
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W6 · Proteomics

1.  Why Measure Proteins 💪 — where the other 80% of protein variance comes from
2.  Mass Spectrometry Basics ⚗️ — the bottom-up workflow, MS2 spectra, DDA vs DIA vs targeted
3.  Identification and Quantification 🏷️ — target–decoy FDR, protein inference, LFQ/TMT/SILAC
4.  The Missing Value Problem 🕳️ — MNAR vs MAR, and why naive imputation is dangerous
5.  Statistical Analysis 📊 — how proteomics differs from RNA-seq statistically
6.  Affinity-Based and Population Proteomics 🩸 — dynamic range, Olink/SomaScan, pQTLs
7.  Frontiers and Pitfalls 🚧 — PTMs, AlphaFold, contamination and pre-analytical variation
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## W7 · Metagenomics

1.  The Human Microbiome 🦠 — body sites, between-person variation, evidence tiers
2.  Study Design and Sample Handling 🧊 — extraction bias, confounders, the kit-ome
3.  Two Ways to Sequence a Community 🧬 — 16S amplicon vs shotgun; OTUs vs ASVs
4.  Reference Databases and Their Limits 📚 — SILVA, GTDB, microbial dark matter
5.  Diversity 🌿 — alpha, beta, rarefaction, PCoA and PERMANOVA
6.  Statistics for Compositional Data ⚠️ — CLR, and why DA methods disagree
7.  From Association to Causation 🔀 — artifact, confounding, reverse causation, causation
8.  Beyond Bacteria, Beyond DNA 🔭 — virome, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics
9.  🎓 **Reading Any Omics Paper Critically** — the closing checklist for the whole course
:::

## 🧵 Three threads that run through every week

Whatever the technology, the same three failure modes recur. Watch for them each week.

+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| Week                   | Confounding             | Multiple testing        | Reference bias      |
+:=======================+:========================+:========================+:====================+
| **W1** Introduction    | batch effects           | FDR vs. Bonferroni      | GRCh38 vs. T2T      |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W2** Genomics        | population structure    | 5×10⁻⁸                  | LD reference panels |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W3** Epigenomics     | cell-type composition   | DMP burden              | chromatin atlases   |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W4** Transcriptomics | batch, RIN, composition | DE gene lists           | annotation version  |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W5** Single-cell     | donor vs. batch         | per-cell inflation      | annotation atlases  |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W6** Proteomics      | TMT batch structure     | peptide vs. protein FDR | search database     |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+
| **W7** Metagenomics    | kit-ome, diet, drugs    | DA method disagreement  | SILVA / GTDB        |
+------------------------+-------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------+

## ⚠️ The traps, by week

If you remember one thing from each chapter, remember these.

+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Week   | The trap                                                                                                                |
+:======:+=========================================================================================================================+
| **W1** | [Batch confounded with condition cannot be fixed by any analysis](chapters/w1_intro.qmd) — randomise your sample layout |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W2** | [The lead SNP is usually not causal, and the nearest gene is often the wrong gene](chapters/w2_genomics.qmd)            |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W3** | [Cell-type composition is the dominant confounder in tissue methylation studies](chapters/w3_epigenomics.qmd)           |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W4** | [Bulk differential expression is frequently a composition difference](chapters/w4_transcriptomics.qmd)                  |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W5** | [Per-cell tests are invalid across conditions — your n is the number of donors](chapters/w5_singlecell.qmd)             |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W6** | [You never observe a protein; naive imputation manufactures false positives](chapters/w6_proteomics.qmd)                |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **W7** | [Sequencing measures proportions, and DA methods disagree on the same data](chapters/w7_metagenomics.qmd)               |
+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

## 🧭 How to read each chapter

Every chapter follows the same shape:

-   **🎯 Learning objectives** — what you should be able to do afterwards
-   **🤔 Motivating question** — the problem the chapter exists to solve
-   **Numbered sections** — `1.` → `1)` → `①`, mirroring the lecture
-   **⚠️ Pitfall boxes** — the mistakes that show up in real manuscripts
-   **💡 Tips** — practical guidance for your own project
-   **📝 Summary · 🔑 Key terms · ➕ References**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Cross-links

Sections marked 🔗 point back to an earlier week. Omics layers are not independent, and the connections are where most of the interesting biology lives — the clearest example runs W2 → W3 → W4 → W6, from a non-coding GWAS hit to a genetically validated drug target.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Where this ends up

The course closes with a checklist in [**W7 §9**](chapters/w7_metagenomics.qmd#w7-s9) for reading any omics paper critically — design, measurement, analysis, interpretation — with pointers back to the chapter that covers each question.

If you can work through that list on a paper in your own field, this course has done its job.
:::
